analysis.one_liner: Narrows approval of OxyContin-type painkillers to severe-only pain to curb abuse.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action after being referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in March 2010, and expired when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the FDA to change the label on controlled-release oxycodone drugs like OxyContin so they could only be approved for severe pain, not moderate-to-severe pain. That change would shrink the number of patients who could legally be prescribed the drug, aiming to reduce diversion and addiction. It died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, particularly in areas hit hard by prescription opioid addiction, would face reduced availability of OxyContin for moderate pain, limiting the pool of pills available for misuse and diversion into illegal markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and communities facing opioid abuse

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FDA to modify approval of controlled-release oxycodone to limit it to severe-only pain instead of moderate-to-severe pain.
Applies the restriction to drugs entering interstate commerce within 180 days of enactment, closing off the large moderate-pain prescribing market that fueled diversion.

analysis.who_pays: Purdue Pharma and other makers of controlled-release oxycodone would lose a large share of their market: patients with moderate pain could no longer be prescribed the drug, shrinking prescriptions and revenue.

drawbacks.text: Patients with moderate-to-severe chronic pain who currently benefit from OxyContin could lose access to a medication their doctors consider appropriate, potentially leaving some with less effective pain relief.

The bill overrides the FDA's usual scientific review process by mandating a label change by statute rather than through the agency's own risk-based evaluation, which some would argue sets a poor precedent for drug regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a real cost — reduced pain treatment options for some patients — for a public-health gain: fewer OxyContin prescriptions overall means fewer pills available for misuse. The mechanism is blunt (a statutory label mandate rather than FDA judgment), and whether narrowing the label materially reduces abuse is uncertain, since opioid dependence is a complex problem not solved by label changes alone. Still, the scale of the eventual opioid epidemic makes this a reasonable attempt to limit supply of a highly abusable drug at the expense of a specific manufacturer's revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing or vote, expiring when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Introduced March 25, 2010 by Rep. Mary Bono Mack (R-CA) with 10 cosponsors split between both parties.
Referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day; no further action was taken.
No committee markup, hearing, floor vote, or Senate action occurred before the 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Purdue Pharma and other controlled-release oxycodone manufacturers benefit, since the bill that would have shrunk their market died without a vote. Public-health groups and communities hit by opioid addiction lost an opportunity to restrict supply of the drug.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid manufacturers; opioid-affected communities lost a tool

for.name: Rep. Mary Bono Mack
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought to narrow OxyContin's approved uses to severe-only pain.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote; its sponsor and cosponsors were mostly Republicans with a couple of Democrats, but no opposition is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Opioid manufacturers (Purdue Pharma and other controlled-release oxycodone makers)
industries.note: The bill would have cut OxyContin's approved market roughly in half by removing moderate-pain patients, directly reducing prescriptions and revenue. The industry had a strong financial interest in the bill dying.
